title: What Are AI Agents?
description: A plain-language explanation of AI agents — what makes them different from chatbots and when they actually help.

data.text: A regular chatbot answers questions. An AI agent actually does things. It can search the web, write and run code, send emails, fill in forms, and chain together multi-step tasks — with minimal human input. Understanding agents helps you use today's most powerful AI tools correctly and safely.

From the original project brief: "A regular chatbot answers questions. An AI agent actually does things." This distinction — response vs. action — is the simplest way to decide whether you need an agent or a chatbot for a given problem.
Chatbot vs Agent

rows: Responds to one message at a time
Plans and executes a whole sequence of steps
Can use tools: search, code, APIs, files, email
Acts autonomously until goal is achieved or stuck
May have persistent memory and task state
Agent gathers additional context itself via tools
Mistakes are contained to one message
Mistakes can cascade across multiple steps

data.text: The agent loop

data.caption: The observe-plan-act cycle every AI agent runs — it loops until the goal is achieved
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  G["Goal given by user\ne.g. 'Research top 5 CRMs\nand compare in a table'"] --> O
  O["Observe: What do I know?\nWhat info is missing?"] --> P
  P["Plan: What tool next?"] --> A
  A["Act: Use a tool\n(search / code / file / API)"] --> R
  R["Read result"] --> E
  E{"Goal achieved?"}
  E -->|No| O
  E -->|Yes| DONE["Return result\nto user"]
  style G fill:#ddf4ff,stroke:#0969da
  style DONE fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37

data.text: Tools agents use

rows: Retrieves current information from the web
Find the latest pricing for Salesforce

Read your PDF, create a report
Fill out forms, extract data from pages
Reads and sends messages, creates events

data.text: Quick start: when to try an agent

items: You need to coordinate multiple tools (search, spreadsheets, email) to complete a task.
The task is repetitive and rule-based but spans systems (e.g., weekly report generation).
You need up-to-date web information and synthesis rather than a single factual answer.
You want to automate a multi-step workflow but keep a human approval gate for final actions.

Low — requires you to approve each step
Autonomous multi-step web research, cited report
Work with your documents persistently across sessions
Draft emails, schedule meetings, create Docs from notes
Medium — can take real actions in your workspace
Read codebase, write new features, run tests

data.title: Agents require more oversight, not less
data.text: Because agents act autonomously across multiple steps, mistakes compound. Always: (1) review before sensitive actions, (2) grant minimum permissions, (3) test on non-critical tasks first, (4) keep humans in the loop for anything irreversible.

data.title: Key concepts
points: Agents plan and execute multi-step tasks using tools — chatbots only respond
The agent loop: observe → plan → act → check goal → repeat
Agents use web search, code execution, file access, browser, and API tools
Higher capability means higher oversight responsibility
You do not need to code to use most agent tools available today

data.text: How agents decide what to do next

Decision-making in agents is a mix of heuristic planning (predefined rules), learned reasoning (LLM-generated plans), and retrieval (fetching relevant memory or documents). Agents often use a scoring function to pick the next action: expected information gain, cost (time/permissions), and risk. Good agent prompts make these trade-offs explicit.

data.caption: Simplified decision scoring for action selection
data.definition:
graph TD
  A["Candidate actions"] --> S["Score: info_gain - cost - risk"]
  S --> B["Select highest score"]
  B --> Execute["Execute action (tool call)"]
  style A fill:#fff3bf,stroke:#d97706
  style Execute fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37

data.text: Memory and retrieval in agents

Agents rely on two complementary memory systems: short-term context (what's in the current conversation and recent tool outputs) and long-term memory (persisted facts, documents, and embeddings). Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the common pattern: retrieve relevant documents from a vector store, then condition the LLM's plan and actions on those documents.

data.caption: Memory retrieval flow: query → retrieve relevant docs → condition plan → act
data.definition:
graph TD
  Q["User query / goal"] --> R["Retrieve relevant docs (vector DB)"]
  R --> L["LLM conditions plan on retrieved context"]
  L --> T["Select tool and act"]
  T --> O["Tool output stored in short-term context"]
  O --> Q

  style Q fill:#fff3bf,stroke:#d97706
  style R fill:#e6f4ff,stroke:#0366d6
  style L fill:#ddf4ff,stroke:#0969da
  style T fill:#fff8c5,stroke:#9a6700

data.text: Safety, permissions, and privacy

Agents can access sensitive systems and data. Design principles: least privilege (grant only required permissions), explicit consent for actions, audit logs of tool calls, and human approval gates for irreversible operations. Sanitize prompts and memories to avoid leaking secrets into tool calls or logs.
When to use agents (and when not to)

rows: Agents reduce manual orchestration and save time
A chatbot is faster and cheaper
Agents can fetch and synthesize up-to-date information
Require human review and deterministic verification
Agents can run reliably with verification and monitoring

data.text: Design patterns for reliable agents

items: Plan-then-act: generate a short plan before calling tools to avoid unnecessary calls
Verify-then-commit: run deterministic checks (schema, calculators) before making changes
Human-in-the-loop: require approval for destructive or irreversible actions
Least-privilege tools: separate read-only and write-capable tool credentials
Memory hygiene: redact or encrypt sensitive fields before storing

data.text: Agent prompt templates (copy-and-adapt)

rows: "Goal: Summarize the top 5 recent developments in [topic] in 500 words. Tools allowed: web_search. Success: 500 words + 3 citations. If a claim is uncertain, mark it 'needs verification'."
Include success criteria and allowed tools
"Goal: Ingest CSV from [url], compute monthly totals, append to [sheet]. Tools allowed: code_executor, sheets_api. Validate totals and flag anomalies >10%."
"Goal: Classify incoming ticket into {billing, technical, account}. Use examples below. If confidence < 0.6, create a 'needs human' ticket."
Combine few-shot examples with confidence threshold

data.text: Concrete examples of agent workflows

data.title: Research assistant (multi-step)
data.content:
Goal: Produce a 500-word brief on recent funding trends in climate tech.

1. Plan: identify subtopics (VC activity, notable rounds, geographic trends).
2. Tools: web search for recent articles; extract key facts; summarize; cite sources.
3. Act: run searches, extract quotes and numbers, draft brief.
4. Check: verify citations and numbers, run a final pass for coherence.

Agent returns a draft with inline citations and a short list of sources.

data.title: Automated spreadsheet update
data.content:
Goal: Update monthly revenue spreadsheet with latest sales data.

1. Plan: fetch sales CSV via API, parse, compute monthly totals, append to sheet.
2. Tools: API call, code execution to compute aggregates, Google Sheets API to write.
3. Check: validate totals against previous month and flag anomalies.

Agent performs the update and flags any discrepancies for human review.

data.text: Common failure modes and how to mitigate them

rows: Agent calls wrong API or uses write permission when read-only was intended
Limit permissions; separate credentials for read/write; include explicit tool descriptions in prompt
An early incorrect result leads to multiple downstream mistakes
Add verification after each critical step; implement rollback or human approval gates
Agent relies on outdated long-term facts
Timestamp memory entries; prefer retrieval freshness checks; refresh embeddings periodically
Agent asserts uncertain facts as truth
Require confidence labels; mark low-confidence claims as 'needs verification'; surface sources
Important context is truncated and the agent loses track
Summarize and compress long context; use retrieval for long-term memory

data.text: How to evaluate agent performance

rows: Percentage of tasks completed correctly end-to-end
Number of tool calls per task and unnecessary calls
How often the agent recovers from tool failures without human help
Are plans and intermediate steps surfaced for inspection?
Does the agent respect data constraints and avoid disallowed actions?

data.text: Agents can act autonomously but are not infallible. Always include verification steps for high-stakes tasks and limit tool permissions to the minimum required.
Audit, logging, and observability

For production agents, capture an immutable audit trail: user goal, plan, each tool call (inputs and outputs), decisions made, and final result. Observability helps debug failures, attribute responsibility, and meet compliance requirements.
Advanced topics to explore

items: Tree-of-Thought planning: structured search over multiple reasoning branches to solve combinatorial problems
Self-reflection and verification loops: agents that critique and improve their own outputs
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): grounding agent decisions in external knowledge stores
Cost-aware planning: include latency and monetary cost in action scoring
Safety frameworks: formalizing permissions, approval gates, and red-team testing for agents

data.text: Best practices for building and using agents

items: Define clear success criteria and stopping conditions for every agent task
Limit tool permissions and scope to reduce risk
Log tool calls and intermediate steps for auditability
Add deterministic verification (calculators, schema checks) for critical outputs
Use self-reflection or re-planning when checks fail
Continuously monitor performance and update memory or prompts when inputs drift

data.text: Advanced prompt templates and patterns

rows: "First list the substeps you will take and the tool for each step. Then execute step 1 and report results."
Avoids unnecessary tool calls and clarifies intent
"After computing or retrieving results, run these checks: [schema checks, numeric validation]. If checks pass, commit changes; otherwise, flag for review."
"Example: [short plan + action + verification]. Example: ... Now for this new goal, produce plan + actions + verification."

rows: Define success criteria and failure modes
Ensures predictable stopping and recovery behavior
Reveals brittle or unsafe behaviors before deployment

data.text: When evaluating an agent, ask: Can it explain its plan? Does it surface intermediate steps? Can I audit its tool calls? These properties are strong indicators of reliability.
Conclusion and next steps

Agents extend LLMs with planning, tools, and memory to solve multi-step tasks. Start by prototyping simple execution loops, add deterministic verification, and progressively enable more autonomy while monitoring safety and performance. For advanced tasks, explore self-reflection, tree-of-thought planning, and retrieval-augmented memories.
